claims.text: Non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys can contain a metastable mixture of solid solutions and intermetallic compounds.
The proposed initial alloy has a homogeneous distribution of Mg.
The proposed alloy has a density below 6 g/cm3.
Thermal exposure causes Mg to diffuse out of the metastable matrix.
Mg redistribution drives nucleation and growth of stable, fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Thermal exposure causes Mg to segregate to grain boundaries.
Mg partitioning into precipitates locally depletes the matrix of Mg.
Mg partitioning enriches surface and interface regions in Mg.
Surface Mg enrichment produces a coherent, protective Mg-enriched oxide scale during high-temperature oxidation.
The protective scale lowers oxidation mass gain or reduces scale spallation relative to the as-cast alloy.
Mg redistribution and the resulting change in local chemistry alter localized corrosion kinetics.
Heat treatment may reduce room-temperature corrosion resistance relative to the as-cast state.
Phase and microstructure evolution depend on temperature and alloy composition.
Induction melting is treated as a rapid, non-equilibrium processing route within the hypothesis boundary.
Additional alloying elements or different processing routes can alter Mg diffusion kinetics and intermetallic-phase stability.

contradictions.description: The intervention says the controlled heat treatment is applied in both oxidizing and corrosive-media environments, whereas the conditions and experiment describe heat treatment in air followed by a separate room-temperature corrosion test. It is therefore unclear whether corrosion occurs during thermal exposure or only after it.
